data.title: Change of Date for Sivers Semiconductors' Q3 2026 Report and Invitation to Presentation
data.description:
KISTA, Sweden, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sivers Semiconductors AB (STO: SIVE) today announced that the Board of Directors has decided to move the publication of the interim report for the third quarter of 2026 from Thursday, November 26, 2026 to Monday, November 30, 2026. The report will be published at approximately 6:00 PM CET (12:00 PM ET), followed by a webcast presentation at 6:30 PM CET (12:30 PM ET).

The original date coincides with the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday, and the new date has been chosen to facilitate participation by the Company's growing base of U.S. investors and analysts. As previously communicated, Sivers publishes its quarterly reports and hosts its webcasts after the close of trading on Nasdaq Stockholm, supporting broad participation across international markets.

The presentation will be held in English by Sivers' management and will be followed by a Q&A session. The report will be available at www.sivers-semiconductors.com, and the webcast can be followed at:

data.title: Nymex Overview: Crude, Refined Products Lower as Supply Concerns Weigh — OPIS
data.description:
Crude futures moved lower with oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and recovering Middle Eastern production continuing to weigh on prices despite lingering concerns over regional conflict.

Both major benchmarks were on track for a third consecutive weekly decline.

January ICE Brent crude was trading 74cts lower at $91.24/bbl on Friday, while the February contract was down 67cts at $88.77/bbl.

December West Texas Intermediate slipped 46cts to $82.75/bbl, with January WTI off 43cts at $82.01/bbl.

Refined product futures were also lower. December ULSD fell 2.05cts to $3.9309/gal, with the January contract down 0.9ct at $3.8524/gal.

The December RBOB contract was trading 1.42cts lower at $2.4809/gal, with January down 1.12cts at $2.4580/gal.

Macquarie Group said resilient flows through the Strait remain a central factor for energy markets, including liquefied natural gas. Continued shipments through the waterway, alongside the persistence of the Iran blockade, could maintain pressure on oil prices, although the potential for further escalation in the region remains a risk, analysts said.

Recent U.S. Energy Information Administration data also point to improving regional supply. Oil shipments through major Middle Eastern chokepoints increased 19% in the third quarter from the previous three months, while regional crude production reached 23.1 million b/d in October, its highest level since the conflict began. EIA expects recovering Middle Eastern production and exports to contribute to rising global inventories, with relatively flat near-term demand.

data.title: MasTec Pasted Despite Murphy Purchase
data.description:
MasTec, Inc. today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Murphy Corporation, one of the largest and most respected mechanical contractors in the United States.

Founded in 1907 and continuously family owned and operated for more than 119 years, Murphy has built a scaled, full-service platform providing mechanical, plumbing and process infrastructure solutions across mission-critical end markets. With approximately 1,200 highly skilled union craft professionals and national execution capabilities, Murphy serves a diversified portfolio of customers in aviation and defense, healthcare, pharmaceutical manufacturing, technology, food processing, refrigeration and advanced manufacturing, supported by industry-leading engineering, preconstruction and fabrication capabilities.

Murphy's experienced management team, led by CEO Patrick Murphy, will remain in place following the Transaction.

In addition to its large-scale construction capabilities, Murphy maintains a substantial service and maintenance business providing recurring HVAC, plumbing, refrigeration, controls and other mechanical services to mission-critical facilities as well as other market sectors.

MasTec believes this business is positioned for significant growth as Murphy expands its owner-direct relationships and supports the increasing number of data centers and other large-load facilities transitioning from construction into ongoing operation. This recurring service revenue complements Murphy’s project-based operations, strengthens customer relationships and enhances the resilience and visibility of its financial performance.

MTZ shares dived $19.76, or 1.2%, to $145.00

data.title: Tech Rout Deepens as Anthropic Stock Slides — WSJ
data.description:
By Ed Ballard

The selloff in technology stocks is intensifying, dragging the S&P 500 and Dow industrials into correction territory.

The Nasdaq is sliding more than 3% as investors continue to pull money out of AI stocks, and Anthropic shares are down 11%, giving up a big chunk of their day-one gains.

The Dow, down about 175 points Friday, and the S&P 500, off about 1.8%, both were recently trading in correction territory, generally defined as 10% or more off a recent peak.

The S&P 500 is headed for its seventh down day in a row, which would be its longest losing streak since 2020. The Dow is down more than 6% for the week.

Investors also are watching whether Anthropic will slip below its IPO price of $83 a share. It was recently near $85.

The Claude maker's blockbuster debut Thursday did little to allay fears about the broader AI trade. "The AI buildout still needs vast amounts of funding just as financing costs are rising and signs of credit stress are emerging," said Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya. The prospect of tighter chip-export rules also is a worry, she added.

U.S. Treasurys are climbing, sending yields lower, as investors seek safe assets. The yield on the 10-year note has dipped below 5%. The dollar is hovering near a one-year high.

Write to Ed Ballard at ed.ballard@wsj.com

data.title: SpaceX-Owned Cursor Considers Dropping Chinese AI Models – A Look At Some Key Details
data.description:
Key points:
  • The report includes 12 policy recommendations aimed at reducing American dependence on Chinese AI technology.
  • Lawmakers recommended keeping China-developed AI models out of federal contract work and high-risk functions of critical infrastructure. 
  • SpaceX acquired Cursor in August in an all-stock transaction for about $60 billion to boost its AI business.

SpaceX’s (SPCX) AI coding platform Cursor is considering dropping Chinese-developed AI models amid geopolitical tensions, according to a congressional report released on Friday.

SPCX shares were down 6.6% at the time of writing.

Cursor Used Kimi K2.5 To Build Coding Model

The report, prepared by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, follows an investigation launched in April into American companies’ use of Chinese AI models and the potential security risks involved.

Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, which built its proprietary Composer 2 coding model using Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.5, informed lawmakers that it plans to explore moving away from Chinese-developed open-weight models.

“Anysphere informed the Committees that it plans to explore phasing out PRC-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk,” the report read.

SpaceX acquired Cursor in August in an all-stock transaction for about $60 billion to boost its AI business.

The investigation also examined Airbnb (ABNB), which uses Alibaba’s (BABA) Qwen models for customer support, and DoorDash (DASH), which has deployed multiple models developed in China.

Washington Pushes For Tighter AI Restrictions

The congressional report includes 12 policy recommendations aimed at reducing American dependence on Chinese AI technology. Among them, lawmakers recommended keeping China-developed AI models out of federal contract work and high-risk functions of critical infrastructure.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is reportedly considering requiring American companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models. The proposal, described as a “name and shame” campaign, aims to discourage reliance on Chinese technology without introducing outright restrictions.

Chinese models have reportedly gained popularity among American businesses because of their lower costs and competitive performance, but Washington remains concerned about security risks and growing dependence on Chinese technology.

data.title: Anthropic Mathematician Says Claude Has Solved the Most Famous Problem in Math — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Cohen

The day after Anthropic's historic IPO, a mathematician who works for the company went public with some history of his own.

He says he has discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis — the most famous unsolved problem in math.

Ever since the Riemann hypothesis was proposed in 1859, a proof of the iconic conjecture in number theory had eluded the brightest human minds. For 167 years, mathematicians tried to crack it. And for 167 years, they all failed. By the time it was selected as one of the seven notoriously difficult Millennium Prize Problems in 2000, it had become known as the field's holy grail. Even the smartest AI models hadn't been able to crack it.

But on Friday, Anthropic's Levent Alpöge revealed that he believes he's found the solution with the help of Claude.

If the proof checks out, it would count as the most remarkable accomplishment in the year of AI's extraordinary math progress. It would also be the second Millennium Prize Problem taken down by artificial intelligence, after an OpenAI model — and millions of dollars in computing power — managed to solve one in September. Humans alone have only solved one of these fiendishly difficult problems.

On his website, Alpöge posted the proof in Lean, a programming language that allows computers to verify it, line by line, and mathematicians immediately got to work trying to wrap their minds around the argument. He said the full argument is both "incredibly long" and "some massive unreadable travesty of 'slop,' " with the AI-written version clocking in at more than 250,000 pages.

The result was achieved late Sunday night into Monday, he said, days before Anthropic went public. Given the timing, which Alpöge called "horrible," he said he messaged CEO Dario Amodei to ask for permission to announce the solution. "The fact is that there was a constraint to respect," Alpöge wrote.

Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment after he posted his findings on Friday morning, as the company's stock price dropped on its first full day of trading.

"I just could not live if I waited even longer," Alpöge wrote.

He added: "In a time of revolution in mathematics I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead, and shows us the joy and wonder we are about to find in the simplest things."

Write to Ben Cohen at ben.cohen@wsj.com

data.title: Buckle Marches on Quarterly Figures
data.description:
The Buckle, Inc. announced today that net income for the fiscal quarter ended October 31, 2026 was $48.0 million, or $0.95 per share ($0.94 per share on a diluted basis).

Net sales for the quarter increased 2.6% to $329.2 million from net sales of $320.8 million for the prior year 13-week fiscal quarter ended November 1, 2025.

Online sales decreased 1.4% to $52.2 million for the 13-week fiscal quarter ended October 31, 2026, compared to net sales of $53.0 million for the 13-week fiscal quarter ended November 1, 2025.

Net income for the third quarter of fiscal 2026 was $48.0 million, or $0.95 per share ($0.94 per share on a diluted basis), compared with net income of $48.7 million, or $0.97 per share ($0.96 per share on a diluted basis) for the third quarter of fiscal 2025.

Buckle is a specialty retailer focused on delivering exceptional service and style through unforgettable experiences. Offering a curated mix of high-quality, on-trend apparel, accessories, and footwear, Buckle is for those living the styled life.

Known as a denim destination, each store carries a wide selection of fits, styles, and finishes from leading denim brands, including the Company’s exclusive brand, BKE.

BKE shares spiked $2.71, or 6.5%, to $44.62.

data.title: Bitcoin falls over 20% in November as ETF outflows mount, but history offers some hope
data.description:
Bitcoin has shed more than 20% of its value in November. It is now trading just under $60,000, which leaves it more than 50% below the all-time high of about $126,000 it set on October 6, 2025.

The slide matters because of when it is happening. Historically, this stretch of the calendar has been kind to Bitcoin holders. Instead, the asset is on track for one of its weakest Novembers in recent years, driven by fund redemptions, a rattled tech sector, and jittery interest rate expectations.

The month started on a much more comfortable note. Bitcoin peaked near $81,000 in the opening days of November before sellers took over.

By November 20, the price had broken below $60,000, with intraday lows landing somewhere between $58,678 and $59,540. That marks the lowest level since early July. One dataset tracking the month-to-date move pegged the drop to around $61,910 at one point, as the slide stair-stepped lower.

The biggest single pressure point appears to be the US spot Bitcoin ETFs. Net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs totaled between $3.47 billion and $3.5 billion in November.

BlackRock's IBIT, the heavyweight of the category, recorded its largest single-day outflow on November 19, at $541 million.

Crypto did not fall in isolation. Technology stocks went through a sharp sell-off tied to a record IPO by Anthropic, the AI company. Interest rates are the other worry. Investors have grown concerned about the possibility of additional Federal Reserve rate hikes.

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, a popular gauge that blends volatility, momentum, and other inputs into a single mood reading, dropped into "extreme fear" territory.

From 2010 through 2025, Bitcoin averaged a 34.4% return in November. It closed the month in positive territory in 10 of those 16 years.

A drop of more than 20% puts the current November firmly in the camp of the six years that ended in the red.

The immediate question for the market is whether the ETF selling has run its course. Spot ETF flows have become one of the clearest real-time signals of institutional appetite for Bitcoin. If redemptions slow or reverse, that would remove one of the main sources of pressure behind this month's decline.

For now, the key things to watch are daily ETF flow data, especially from IBIT, any shift in Federal Reserve expectations, and whether the broader tech sell-off stabilizes.

data.title: One Potential Factor Weighing on Meta Shares Today: a Job Posting at Apple — WSJ
data.description:
By Rolfe Winkler

While the slide in Anthropic shares and broader tech selloff are dragging down Meta's stock (down about 4% today), a new competitive threat from Apple may also be having an impact.

An Apple job posting from this week suggests the company might be aiming to build a tool similar to Meta's viral Muse AI agent tool.

The posting for a "Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI - Proactive" that went up earlier this week read as follows:

  • Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we're looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.

That sounds like Apple is working on an AI tool to complete tasks for users, similar to ones already released by Apple's rivals. Besides Muse there is SpaceXAI's GrokBot, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Claude Duet, and the recently released "Gemini Tasks" from Google, as well as one from the viral startup Instinct. Such tools can book flights, fill out online forms, send emails, and communicate with customer service agents, all on a user's behalf.

Bloomberg first reported the senior engineering manager role late yesterday. It was removed from Apple's site shortly after. An Apple spokeswoman didn't immediately reply to a request for comment.

Apple has Siri, which is now a more competent chatbot thanks to a fall update. But Siri remains woefully behind when it comes to completing tasks. Apple seems to be investing in that gap. Among the hundreds of job postings it has put out in recent weeks are a handful that describe work in the area. Another that is still live seeks someone to work on "self-improving agentic systems."

data.title: AAII investors grow less pessimistic, but bears still dominate
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq slides >3%, S&P 500 down ~2%; Dow dips, but now on track for correction
  • Tech, down ~5%, weakest S&P 500 sector; consumer staples leads gainers
  • STOXX 600 index falls 2%
  • Dollar down; US crude dips; gold falls >2%; bitcoin loses >3%
  • US 10-year Treasury yield falls to ~4.94%

AAII INVESTORS GROW LESS PESSIMISTIC, BUT BEARS STILL DOMINATE

Individual investors grew less pessimistic this week according to the latest American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) sentiment survey released on Thursday. Bullish and neutral sentiment both improved, while bearishness declined, although pessimism remained elevated by historical standards.

Bullish sentiment, which reflects expectations that stock prices will rise over the next six months, increased 2.6 percentage points to 33.3%. Even so, it remained below its historical average of 37.5% for the fourth time in five weeks.

Neutral sentiment posted the largest gain, rising 6.7 percentage points to 24.4%. Despite the increase, it stayed below its historical average of 31.0% for a 37th consecutive week.

Bearish sentiment, meanwhile, slid 9.2 percentage points to 42.2%. While that marked a notable decline, bearish sentiment remained unusually high, staying above its historical average of 31.5% for a 41st straight week.

As a result, the bull-bear spread, a measure of overall sentiment, improved to negative 8.9% from negative 20.6% last week. Even so, the spread remained below its historical average of positive 6.5% for an 18th consecutive week.

In this week's special question, AAII members were asked whether they believe other investors are currently too bullish or too bearish. The largest share of respondents, just over one-third, said investors are too bearish right now.

data.title: Arizona AG asks local zoning board to delay vote on SpaceX's $50B data center: report
data.description:
Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes has requested a local zoning commission in the state to tap the brakes on an upcoming vote for SpaceX's proposed $50B data center, according to Bloomberg.

The Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to vote on a special use permit for the facility on December 9.

"This delay is necessary to ensure that the County does not begin authorizing a project with potentially far-reaching impacts on the region's energy reliability, water availability, and resident health and safety until it has been thoroughly vetted by the relevant state and federal regulatory authorities," Mayes said in a letter to commissioners, according to the report.

Mayes plans to hold a community meeting in the county on December 3.

"Working with local electric cooperatives, the project aims to strengthen regional energy infrastructure, leverage existing renewable resources, and potentially reduce electricity bills for cooperative members by up to 20% while using dry cooling with no planned industrial groundwater consumption," SpaceX said of the project.

SpaceX is also in the process of adding $24B in AI infrastructure at its facility in Brownsville, Texas. Earlier this week, Cameron County Commissioners voted against moving forward on a hearing to consider a tax abatement on the new data center.

"Property owners could now face greater year-to-year fluctuations in tax rates as the equipment depreciates," SpaceX said of the decision in a post on X. "The agreement was intended to provide more predictable County revenue while supporting continued investment in the region. We look forward to continued discussions with local jurisdictions on how to maximize the economic benefits of these investments while protecting sustainable, long-term tax revenues."

SpaceX shares declined nearly 7% by noon trading on Friday.

data.title: Europe's cheap-labour edge fades as emerging markets catch up - IntelliNews Lambda
data.description:
Europe is being forced to shut down factories because it can no longer afford its workers. For centuries, its superior productivity added value that fuelled exports and made the continent rich. But as the Global South catches up and starts to overtake the developed countries, rising costs and stagnant productivity has upended the equation. Factories in the heartland spend at least 60 cents on labour for every euro they earn from sales and is rising. An hour of factory labour costs €49.50 in Germany and €15.60 in Hungary, but per euro of output the Hungarian worker is now slightly dearer, Eurostat data show.

Mercedes-Benz is moving production of the A-Class to Kecskemet in central Hungary, already its biggest plant in Europe, and BMW opened a €2bn factory in Debrecen in 2025, while China's BYD is building its first European car plant in Szeged. The pay gap looks like reason enough. Eurostat's labour cost levels survey puts the hourly cost of a manufacturing worker in 2025, wages plus social charges, at €49.50 in Germany, €47.10 in France and an EU average of €35.00, against €20.20 in Czechia, €19.30 in Slovakia, €17.10 in Poland, €15.60 in Hungary, €12.00 in Romania and €10.20 in Bulgaria.

That gap built the modern world economy. For two centuries the West paid its workers far more than anyone else and stayed ahead because they produced far more per hour, with better machines, better training and better technology. When that stopped being enough, western companies moved the labour-intensive work to cheaper countries - globalisation to shareholders, neo-colonialism to critics who argue the West is bleeding the Global South of wealth through wage inequality. The problem for developed markets now is that emerging markets are closing the gap on productivity and technology while their wages remain a fraction of western levels. Across emerging Europe, however, wages have caught up faster than output, and the cost advantage that pulled factories east in the 1990s has largely been spent.

The cost of a euro of output

Pay is only half the sum. Divide Eurostat's national accounts figure for manufacturing value added by the hours worked in factories and a German hour produced €78.80 of value added in 2025, against €29.70 in Czechia, €22.60 in Hungary, €20.30 in Poland, €19.10 in Romania and €13.60 in Serbia. Set the labour cost against that output and the gap shrinks. German manufacturers spent 63 cents on labour for every euro of value added; Romania's spent 63 cents, Czechia's 68 cents, Hungary's 69 cents, Slovakia's 72 cents and Poland's 84 cents, according to IntelliNews calculations from the Eurostat data.

Manufacturing labour cost and gross value added per hour worked, €, 2025 (Bulgaria 2024), with labour cost per €1 of value added. Source: Eurostat; IntelliNews calculations

A Hungarian factory hour costs 32% of a German one and produces 29% as much value. The national averages hide a split economy. They mix foreign-owned assembly plants, built with the same kit as their sister plants in Germany, with smaller and older local firms, so the output of a line in Kecskemet sits well above the Hungarian average. The carmakers keep coming. Mercedes has turned out more than 2mn vehicles in Hungary since 2012, has put €1bn into the plant since 2022 and is opening an R&D centre there with a €54.5mn investment. The automotive sector accounts for a quarter of Hungary's industrial output.

How Central Europe won the first round

In 2008, the first year with comparable data, the sums looked very different. German factories then spent 71 cents on labour per euro of value added, while Slovakia's spent 54 cents, Hungary's 57 cents, Czechia's 60 cents and Romania's just 36 cents. Hourly labour cost €7.00 in Slovakia, €7.50 in Hungary, €8.70 in Czechia and €3.30 in Romania against €32.30 in Germany, between a tenth and just over a quarter of the German level. The workforce, schooled in the heavy industry of the Warsaw Pact economies, was far closer to western skill levels than its pay suggested. That bargain drew Volkswagen to Bratislava and Mlada Boleslav, Audi to Gyor and, later, Mercedes to Kecskemet.

Since then wages have run ahead of output. Hourly labour costs in Czech manufacturing rose by 132% between 2008 and 2025, Hungary's more than doubled and Romania's more than tripled, while Germany's rose by 53%. Value added per hour in Hungarian manufacturing stayed at 29% of the German level over the same period. Czech inward investment halved in 2018 as companies complained they could not find workers, and the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies (wiiw) warned in 2024 that the region needed a new industrial policy to escape the middle-income trap, because its role as an 'extended workbench' for western firms was reaching its limits.

Manufacturing labour cost per €1 of gross value added, euro cents, 2008 and 2025. Serbia starts in 2012, Bulgaria ends in 2024. Source: Eurostat; IntelliNews calculations

Germany's own figure has fallen, from 71 cents to 63, because the value of what its factories produce per hour rose by 29% between 2020 and 2025 while hourly labour costs rose by 18%. Spain, at 60 cents, is now the cheapest place in this group to turn an hour of factory labour into value added. None of that has saved German jobs. Volkswagen's restructuring plan to 2030 envisages around 50,000 job cuts on top of the 70,000 already announced, with four German plants at risk, and its Audi plant in Gyor may also be on the list.

CountryLabour cost per hour 2025, €Value added per hour 2025, €Labour cost per €1 of value added, 2008Labour cost per €1 of value added, 2025Labour cost per hour, change since 2008
Germany49.578.871c63c+53%
France47.167.975c69c+44%
Spain28.247.268c60c+39%
Czechia20.229.760c68c+132%
Slovakia19.326.754c72c+176%
Poland17.120.376c84c+151%
Hungary15.622.657c69c+108%

Manufacturing. Labour cost covers firms with 10 or more employees; value added per hour is gross value added divided by hours worked in the national accounts. Source: Eurostat; IntelliNews calculations

The Balkans take their turn

The Western Balkans were the next layer down. In 2016 an hour of manufacturing labour cost €1.80 in Albania, €2.90 in North Macedonia, €3.90 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and €4.40 in Serbia, against €10.20 in Czechia. The usual explanation for why investors nonetheless preferred Central Europe is that low skills made cheap Balkan labour a false economy. The aggregate data do not bear that out. In 2016 Serbian factories spent 45 cents on labour per euro of value added and Albania's 48 cents, both below Czechia's 58 cents. What held investors back appears to have been what averages do not capture: thin supplier networks, poor roads and rail, political risk and a small pool of trained workers. Output per worker across the whole Serbian economy, adjusted for prices, is 37% of the US level, against 63% in Czechia, on World Bank data.

The investment has since arrived. wiiw identified concrete cases of nearshoring in five of the six Western Balkan economies in 2024, many of them by Asian companies placing factories close to the EU's core. Stellantis now builds the Fiat Grande Panda and Citroen C3 at Kragujevac, where output is close to 500 cars a day. Its Serbian unit swung to a net profit of RSD3.71bn (€31.6mn) in 2025, the country's automotive cluster lifted exports by 51% and cars now make up around 16% of Serbian exports. Serbia has had to look abroad for workers to staff the plant.

Success has raised the bill. Serbia's hourly manufacturing labour cost almost tripled between 2016 and 2025 to €12.00, level with Romania's, and the average gross wage reached RSD168,008 (€1,429) in April. With factory value added of €13.60 an hour, Serbian manufacturers now spend 88 cents on labour for every euro of value added, more than any Central European economy except Croatia.

On these numbers the Balkans have not overtaken Central Europe as the more profitable place to build. The wage advantage is moving south and east faster than productivity is following it, and investors are looking further afield, to Morocco, whose automotive exports rose 14.5% to MAD116bn ($11.6bn) in the first eight months of 2026, and to Mexico, where the nearshoring boom has run into US tariffs.

Half the world's factories are still rich

The idea that the West has exported most of its manufacturing does not survive the data. High-income economies produced 52% of the world's manufacturing value added in 2024, on the World Bank's development indicators, down from 77% in 2004. China's share rose from 8.5% to 28%, after peaking at 30% in 2021, and the rest of the emerging and developing world's from 14% to 20%. The US alone accounted for 15.5% in 2021, the last year the World Bank series covers, and the EU for 17% in 2024. The figures are in current dollars, so exchange rates move them, but the rich world still makes about half of everything manufactured, not a fifth.

Share of world manufacturing value added, %, current dollars, 2004-2024. Source: World Bank World Development Indicators; IntelliNews calculations

What the West exported was the labour-intensive end of the chain: assembly, garments, consumer electronics. Apple designs the iPhone in California and has it assembled in China and, increasingly, India. An iPhone built in the US would cost around $3,500, more than three times the price of a current model, Wedbush Securities analyst Dan Ives told CNN in April 2025. The shift in manufacturing weight is one reason the Kremlin has bet on what it presents as a Global South century.

The catch-up is real, but not everywhere

On the World Bank's measure of GDP per person employed, adjusted for price differences, China has gone from 3.6% of the US level in 1991 to 31% in 2025, Vietnam from 6% to 18% and India from 7% to 16%. Poland has risen from 32% to 62%, Turkey from 39% to 60% and Romania from 35% in 2000 to 64%. Germany has slipped from parity with the US in the early 1990s to 80%.

Not every emerging market is converging. Brazil has fallen from 35% of the US level to 27%, Mexico from 55% to 31% and South Africa from 41% to 31% since 1991. North Macedonia, at 42%, is roughly where it was in 1991. The catch-up story belongs to China, emerging Europe, Turkey and parts of South and Southeast Asia, not to emerging markets as a class.

GDP per person employed, % of the US level, constant 2021 PPP dollars, 1991-2025. Source: World Bank World Development Indicators; IntelliNews calculations

The research race

The bigger shift is in technology, and there China stands apart. It spent CNY3.93 trillion ($589bn) on research and development in 2025, or 2.80% of GDP, the National Bureau of Statistics said in its annual communique on October 16. Eurostat's R&D statistics put China's 2024 spending at €466bn against €408bn for the entire EU. China's R&D spending passed the EU's as a share of GDP in 2020 and reached 2.69% in 2024 against the EU's 2.26%. China filed 25% of the world's patent applications in 2021 against 21% for the US and 17% for the EU, and has overtaken the US in the Nature Index of high-quality research output.

Europe's weakness is the subject of Mario Draghi's report on European competitiveness, published in September 2024. EU companies spent €270bn less on research and innovation than their US counterparts in 2021, it found, and the top three R&I spenders in Europe have been carmakers for the past 20 years, while in the US they are now all tech companies. Implementing Draghi's recommendations could lift the economies of the EU's eastern members, the EBRD's chief economist Beata Javorcik said in October 2024.

The claim that emerging markets as a group now out-invest the West in research does not hold beyond China. South Korea, at 4.94% of GDP in 2023, and Israel, at 6.35%, lead the world, but both are rich economies. India spent 0.65% of GDP on R&D in 2020, its latest figure, Brazil 1.19%, Turkey 1.42%, Vietnam 0.41% and Mexico 0.27%, all well below the EU's 2.26% and the US' 3.45%. In Central Europe Poland spent 1.56% and Hungary 1.38%, according to the World Bank's R&D series.

Gross domestic spending on research and development, % of GDP, 1996-2023. Source: World Bank World Development Indicators

Some of the research is starting to follow the factories. Besides Mercedes' Kecskemet centre, BYD has moved its European headquarters to Hungary and is building a €250mn business and development centre in Budapest that it says will employ 2,000 people, around 90% of them graduates, mainly engineers. For three decades the bargain was western brains and eastern hands. The hands have got dearer, and the brains, in China at least, are no longer a western monopoly.

data.title: Flight to safety drives Treasury yields lower as tech tumbles
data.description:
U.S. Treasury yields declined across the curve on Friday afternoon as equity markets came under pressure, prompting investors to shift into government bonds for relative safety.

The move reflected a classic flight-to-quality response. With stocks selling off, demand for Treasuries increased, driving yields lower.

The front end of the curve led the decline: the U.S. 2-year Treasury yield fell 11 basis points to 4.65%, the largest drop among the major maturities. The benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield dropped 10 basis points to 4.94%, while the longer-end U.S. 30-year Treasury yield eased 7 basis points to 5.33%.

The coordinated retreat underscored heightened caution among market participants. Bond purchases accelerated as equity losses mounted, tightening yields, especially in shorter-dated paper that is more sensitive to near-term shifts in risk appetite and rate expectations.

The session illustrated the ongoing interplay between equities and fixed income. When stock prices weaken, Treasuries frequently absorb the resulting capital flows, producing the inverse relationship observed Friday.

20 November 2026 – SmartCraft Group AB (publ) (“SmartCraft” or the “Company”) has, between 12 November 2026 and 20 November 2026, carried out synthetic repurchases of a total of 1,530,300 ordinary shares under the synthetic share buyback programme resolved upon by the Board of Directors.

On 5 November 2026, SmartCraft announced that the Board of Directors, pursuant to the authorisation granted by the Extraordinary General Meeting held on 29 April 2026, had resolved to initiate a synthetic share buyback programme and enter into an agreement with DNB Carnegie Investment Bank AB (publ) (“DNB Carnegie”) to enable synthetic repurchases of SmartCraft’s ordinary shares on Nasdaq Stockholm. The programme covers synthetic repurchases for an aggregate amount of up to SEK 120 million and a maximum of 6,990,277 ordinary shares. The purpose of the programme is to enable SmartCraft to continuously adjust its capital structure and thereby contribute to increased shareholder value.

SmartCraft’s shares have been repurchased as follows:

All repurchases have been carried out by DNB Carnegie on Nasdaq Stockholm. DNB Carnegie’s holding in SmartCraft thus amounts to 3,311,666 shares, corresponding to 1.92 percent of all shares and 2.05 percent of all votes in the Company. The total number of shares in SmartCraft is 172,836,805, comprising 171,522,305 ordinary shares and 1,314,500 C1-shares. SmartCraft currently holds 10,293,403 of its own ordinary shares.

For further information about the Board of Directors’ decision to initiate the synthetic share buyback programme, please refer to SmartCraft’s press release dated 5 November 2026.

Full details of the transactions carried out are attached to this press release.

About Us

SmartCraft is a Northern European vertical SaaS company providing business-critical software for tradespeople and construction businesses, helping them improve productivity, margins, and resource efficiency. Today, the Group has more than 13,700 customers and 270 employees across Norway, Sweden, Finland, Ireland and the UK. SmartCraft was listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange in June 2021 and subsequently listed on Nasdaq Stockholm in 2026.

data.title: New Mexico high court must face DOJ lawsuit over lawyer licensing of military spouses
data.description:
By Karen Sloan

The US Department of Justice can move ahead with its lawsuit against the New Mexico Supreme Court over its refusal to recognize the out-of-state law licenses of military servicemembers and their spouses, a federal judge has ruled.

US District Judge Kea Riggs on Thursday denied motions to dismiss the case by the state's high court and the New Mexico Board of Bar Examiners, finding that state supreme courts are covered by the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act — a federal law that gives legal and financial protections to military personnel.

“If state supreme courts are not covered by the SCRA, the law would be unlikely to apply to law licenses anywhere,” the judge wrote.

Riggs also ruled that the Justice Department has standing to sue because it adequately alleged a pattern of SCRA violations.

A court spokesperson did not immediately provide comment on Friday. The executive director of the Board of Bar Examiners declined to comment. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit in June, citing the defendants' determination in 2024 that Liam Lees, a UK-trained lawyer whose spouse was transferred to an Air Force base in the state, was ineligible to practice in New Mexico because he has only a one-year master's degree from a US law school and not a full US law degree.

That denial violated the SCRA, which gives servicemembers and military spouses the right to transfer professional licenses between states, the Justice Department alleged.

The New Mexico Supreme Court argued it is not a “licensing authority” under the SCRA because lawyer admissions is not its sole purpose. Riggs disagreed, finding that lawyer licensing and regulation is an “integral part” of the court’s work. She ruled that the Board of Bar Examiners is a subsidiary of the New Mexico Supreme Court and must also face the lawsuit.
